items.excerpt: (Bloomberg) -- Anxiety about inflation has yet to spoil the spending appetite of US consumers in the period leading up to the holiday-shopping season. Economists estimate inflation-adjusted personal spending rose by 0.1% in October from a month earlier, based on the Bloomberg survey's median estimate ahead of government figures due Wednesday. The modest increase builds on two robust quarters of consumer spending growth. The report, the highlight of a Thanksgiving holiday-shortened trading week, is also expected to show an acceleration in inflation. The personal consumption expenditures price index — the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation metric — is projected to rise 3.8% from October of last year. That's nearly double the Fed's goal and would match May as the biggest annual increase in three years. The core measure, which excludes the volatile food and energy categories, is also seen quickening, adding to evidence that Fed officials will raise interest rates at their December meeting. items.title: House Democrats split over risking lame-duck shutdown to defund Iran war
items.excerpt: House Democrats are wrestling with a lame-duck strategy on the Iran war, divided over whether to demand an end to war funding, which could risk triggering a government shutdown — or punting that fight to next year, when they’ll control Congress. On one side of the debate are liberals who, emboldened by this month’s midterm landslide, want to use the Democrats’ leverage in the government funding battle to deny the Pentagon any more money to conduct the war. “We’re going to fight to get that Iran funding removed for offensive military capability,” said Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.). On the other side are top Democrats, including the lead negotiators on the spending package, who also oppose the war but aren’t ready to shutter the government over defunding it. “I frankly want to … end the funding to the Iran War. But shutting the government down doesn’t stop the war,” said Rep. Rosa DeLauro (Conn.), the senior Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee. That internal clash has been playing out for several weeks on the other side of the Capitol, where Senate Democrats are also at odds over how aggressively to pursue the defund-the-war strategy in the lame duck session — a debate that’s grown only more salient after Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) launched a challenge to Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for the top leadership spot next year. Van Hollen has positioned himself to the left of Schumer, and his demand to halt war funding immediately — even if it leads to a government shutdown — has energized the Democrats’ liberal base even as it has divided the party on Capitol Hill. The midterm results have fueled that clash, providing the Van Hollen camp with a powerful argument: Voters demanded this. The divisions on the House side have, so far, been less prominent. But as the government spending debate inches closer to the Dec. 11 shutdown deadline, liberals in the lower chamber are making clear that they’re on Van Hollen’s side, ready to oppose any spending package that continues to fund the Iran conflict. Asked if the issue is a red line, Khanna, a vice chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, didn’t hesitate. “Yes,” he said. “I do think we’ve got to get that money out.” DeLauro disagreed, arguing that Democrats will fight to end the war, but won’t die on that hill in the lame duck — not least because she doesn’t want a shutdown to delay the Democrats’ legislative agenda in January when they will take control of both chambers of Congress. “It’s not a red line,” she said. “I think we’re trying to get done what we can get done. Because we have a very important agenda to address — affordability and accountability — and we’re ready to do that. And I do not want to delay that.” DeLauro suggested Democrats are eying other strategies for ending the war that don’t risk a shutdown. She did not specify what those are, however, and many Democrats view Congress’s power of the purse as the most forceful tool they have at their disposal. “They want to end this war, and they want to see an end to the funding. The other issue is: How do you strategically move to get that done?” she said. “And that’s what we’re looking at — without shutting down the government.” Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), who’s in line to chair the House Foreign Affairs Committee next year, has been a part of those talks. He suggested Democrats are searching for ways to restrict President Trump’s military operations against Iran in lieu of a complete defunding, which would likely be opposed by Republicans and could trigger a shutdown. “She’s working very hard to get this thing resolved, understanding that we just can’t give the president a blank check,” Meeks said of DeLauro. “You can’t [have a shutdown]. But having amendments and having conditions I think are important also, understanding that come the 120th Congress, we’re in full control, and right now we’re not.” “So we’ve got to figure it out.” That strategy would anger the Democrats’ activist base, who are clamoring for an immediate end to an unpopular war that was a major factor driving the midterm rout. But top Democrats say it’s also the most pragmatic route, empowering Democrats to hit the ground running — and not be bogged down in shutdown politics — when they do take power in January. “You’re going to have to get to the point where you defund it. I would like it to be in the lame duck. But, again, we have to see what are the options here, and what’s moving and what’s not moving,” said Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.). “Starting the new Congress with a government shutdown is not a good idea.”

items.title: Entertainment news roundup: 22 November 2026 | SVCZZ
items.excerpt: ## Sunrise on the Reaping sets the biggest UK opening day of 2026 The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping took $8.2 million on its opening day in the UK, the biggest of 2026 so far, passing Spider-Man: Brand New Day at $7.8 million, Fiction Horizon reports. It had already taken $21 million in Thursday previews in the US, and ScreenRant projects more than $120 million domestic for the opening weekend as of Saturday morning, with final numbers due Monday. Yesterday’s roundup carried the $51 million Friday projection; our reviews piece has the critics split at 67% on Rotten Tomatoes. ## O.M Chapter 1 opens with Rs 19.75 crore in India on day 1 O.M Chapter 1 opened with Rs 19.75 crore in India on day 1, 20 November 2026, Dhanush’s biggest opener, Pinkvilla reports from trade estimates. Production house Wunderbar Films announced over Rs 40 crore worldwide gross on day 1. ## Helen Fraser dies aged 84 Helen Fraser, best known as Bad Girls prison officer Sylvia Hollamby in all eight series, has died aged 84, The Sun reports. She died on 10 November 2026 at Yaxley House Care Home in Eye, Suffolk, The Oldham Times reports, and was also a two-time Coronation Street guest. No cause of death was given. ## Robin Varghese dies aged 56 Robin Varghese, the Malayalam actor known as Shelly in the 1992 Mammootty film Johny Walker, has died aged 56, the Times of India reports from Manorama Online, with NewsBytes also reporting the death. He died in the United States on 19 November 2026. No cause of death was given. ... ## Onslaught streams on HBO Max from 22 December A24’s Onslaught streams on HBO Max from 22 December 2026, ScreenRant reports, after its 4 September 2026 theatrical run and 6 October 2026 digital debut. The date was announced on 20 November 2026. ## Mission: Cross 2 sets a December 2026 Netflix window Mission: Cross 2 has set a December 2026 Netflix release window after a delay from its Q3 2026 slot, What’s on Netflix reports. Hwang Jung Min and Yeom Jung Ah return, with four cast additions, and no exact date has been announced. ... ## Bhogi locks a 27 November release date Sharwanand film Bhogi has locked a new worldwide release date of 27 November 2026, Gulte reports, after the CBFC revising committee cleared it with an A certificate. The makers announced the date on 19 November 2026 after its 12 November release was postponed, with a trailer launch and pre-release event reported for today, 22 November.
